units.title: Did Jesus Really Exist in History?
units.sub: Even Roman historians who looked down on Christians wrote His name. How much can history tell us, and where does it stop?

share.v: The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

blocks.h: Around AD 116, the Roman senator Tacitus was writing a history of the empire. He had no sympathy for Christians and called their faith a harmful superstition. Yet when he came to Nero’s persecution of the Christians, he stopped to explain where they came from: the name came from Christ, who was put to death by Pilate in the reign of Tiberius.
A man who disliked Christians, with no intention of speaking up for anyone, left behind this one line. And so the story of the faith received a date stamp from an outsider.
Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea
Records left by people who did not believe

Tacitus’ Annals 15.44 tells how, after the great fire of Rome in AD 64, Nero shifted the blame onto the Christians, and it explains that Christ was executed by Pilate in the time of Tiberius. Researchers almost all hold that this passage came from Tacitus himself. Robert Van Voorst points out that among Roman writers, Tacitus gives the most precise information about Christ.

The Jewish historian Josephus finished his Antiquities of the Jews in AD 93–94. Book 20, section 200, records that the high priest Ananus had “the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James” put to death. This passage is accepted almost unanimously by scholars.

Pliny the Younger, while governor of Bithynia (around the early AD 110s), wrote to the emperor Trajan to ask how Christians should be handled. He described them meeting before dawn and singing hymns to Christ “as to a god.” The letter says nothing about the life of Jesus, but it shows that less than a hundred years after His death, the people who worshiped Him were numerous enough to alarm a governor.

Picture two families in a small town who have an old feud. One writes to the mayor: “It’s all that Wang fellow’s fault!” That letter cannot prove Mr. Wang is a good man, or even prove what he did, but it is enough to convince you that there really is such a person in town. A hostile document is often the document least in need of the question “Did this person exist?”
The earliest clue is actually in Paul’s hands

Earlier than any of these Roman writings are the letters of Paul. In Galatians, Paul mentions going up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas (Peter) and also “James, the Lord’s brother,” within a few years of Jesus’ death. A man who existed only in myth would hardly have a younger brother leading the church in Jerusalem.

This is why Bart Ehrman, a New Testament scholar who does not believe in Christianity, wrote an entire book, Did Jesus Exist?, to refute the claim that Jesus never existed. He describes himself as an agnostic and does not accept the deity of Jesus, but he maintains that Jesus really lived. James Dunn says that Jesus’ baptism by John and His crucifixion under Pilate are among the facts of history that can hardly be denied.
What the mythicists say
To be honest, some scholars do hold a different view. Below are the strongest arguments on both sides, side by side.

items.h: Tacitus wrote about 80 years after Jesus and may simply be repeating what Christians said; the Josephus passage has been altered; Paul’s letters say very little about Jesus’ earthly life; the Gospels are works of faith. Richard Carrier’s 2014 book, published by an academic press, uses Bayesian probability to argue that Jesus began as a heavenly figure and was only later written into history.

Ancient history rarely has contemporary documents about a preacher from a remote region, and records written decades later are the norm. Paul knew Jesus’ brother and Peter, and Jews would not have invented a crucified Messiah out of thin air. Daniel Gullotta, in the Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus in 2017, answered Carrier point by point and concluded that his assumptions are hard to sustain. On this point, believing and unbelieving scholars mostly stand on the same side.

blocks.h: Three places for caution

First, the famous passage in Josephus’ Antiquities 18.63–64. Most scholars think it has an original core, but that phrases such as “he was the Christ” were added by Christian copyists. John Meier’s reconstruction is the one most often cited. A minority, such as Ken Olson and the later Louis Feldman, argue that the whole passage was added by others. Alice Whealey, who studied the Syriac and Arabic versions, thinks the original may have read “he was thought to be the Christ.” This passage should not be used as “iron-clad proof.”

Second, Suetonius says that Claudius expelled the Jews because of agitation instigated by a man called “Chrestus.” Some think this is a misspelling of Christ, while others think it is simply a different man with the same name. This clue should be treated with doubt. As for the mention in the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a, of a “Yeshu” executed on the eve of Passover, Peter Schäfer regards it as late polemical writing influenced by the Gospels, not an independent source; some scholars think it refers to someone else.

Third, an inscription unearthed at Caesarea in 1961 confirms that Pilate really was governor of Judea, with the title “prefect.” Tacitus calls him “procurator,” which shows that the historian used the title of his own day, and his source was not necessarily the records of the time. Where his information came from is still disputed. In addition, the census of Quirinius in Luke 2:2 has a timing difficulty with the date of AD 6 that Josephus gives; each proposed explanation has its own problems, and there is no settled answer.
This topic deserves that we separate what is certain from what is inferred.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44, records that Christ was executed by Pilate in the time of Tiberius; scholars almost unanimously regard the passage as genuinely his.
Josephus, Antiquities 20.200, mentions James, the brother of Jesus, and is almost universally accepted.
That Jesus really existed, was baptized by John and was crucified under Pilate is the shared conclusion of secular and Christian scholars; those who deny it are a small minority.
That Josephus 18.63–64 has an original core that was later altered is the majority view; other scholars argue that the whole passage was added by others.
Whether Suetonius’ “Chrestus” refers to Jesus, whether the Talmud passage has historical value, and the exact date of the census Luke records are all unsettled.

History can only tell us that this man existed, was executed and left behind a movement; whether He is the Son of God, the historical method cannot decide. Christians believe that God chose to enter real history, with its dates and the names of its officials.
Existence is one thing; deity is another

Ehrman is fully convinced that Jesus existed, yet he does not believe He is God. This reminds us that proving “there was such a man” still leaves a distance before faith. The remaining units of this hall will walk that distance step by step.
God chose a way that can be checked

The Bible pins the story of salvation to years and to the names of officials. Luke lists Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, Annas and Caiaphas, which amounts to handing his book over to later generations to be checked. Pilate’s name can even be found on an inscription.
But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman, born under the law
Here is God’s faithfulness: His promise did not remain an idea in the clouds. At a real time He came into the human world, born to a woman.
The Word became flesh and lived among us.
One event, two ways of writing it
Tacitus wrote Jesus’ death as the end of the leader of a wicked cult. Paul wrote about the very same cross, but with an entirely different meaning:
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures

A historian can record “He died,” but only the gospel can tell you “for whom He died.” He came into the world and willingly let a Roman official condemn Him, so that condemned people could receive forgiveness. The last question is not in the Roman archives. It has to be asked of you and me.

Open to Luke 3:1 and slowly read that string of emperors and officials. Then add in your heart today’s date and your own name. The Lord who walked into the age of Tiberius also walks into this year of yours.
Meditate: Is the Jesus I believe in the real One who walked through the dust of Galilee, or a warm idea in my mind?

Pray: Lord Jesus, thank You that You did not leave behind only an idea but came in person to the human world and suffered under Pilate. Let me know the real You, and let my faith stand up to examination. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: Faith need not fear investigation. When a question comes up, go to the primary sources, and be honest about what is still unresolved.
Jesus is my example: He walked into a real time and place. Today I too will live out my faith in a specific office, at a specific dinner table, among specific neighbors.
Change your mindset: Move from “Jesus is a story” to “Jesus is a real person I must respond to.” When the mindset changes, life and daily living change with it.

blocks.h: This week: Read a translation of Tacitus, Annals 15.44, once, and then read Luke 3:1-2. Write down your single biggest question and bring it to the next unit.
Pass it on: “Even historians who do not believe in Christianity think Jesus was a real person. If you could ask Him one question, what would it be?”
Quiz

quiz.q: What is most remarkable about Tacitus’ account of Christ in Annals 15.44?
o: The author was a Christian, so he recorded it in the greatest detail
The author was hostile to Christians, yet still recorded that Christ was executed by Pilate
The author personally witnessed the crucifixion
quiz.e: Tacitus called this faith a harmful superstition and had no intention of testifying for the Christians. Nor was he an eyewitness.

quiz.q: Which statement about Josephus, Antiquities 18.63–64, is the most honest?
o: Most scholars think it has an original core that Christians later added to
Scholars agree the whole text is unchanged, word for word
All scholars think the entire passage is a forgery
quiz.e: That it is partly authentic is the majority opinion, and a minority of scholars think the whole passage was added later, so it should not be treated as iron-clad proof.

quiz.q: What is Ehrman’s position in Did Jesus Exist?
o: As a Christian, he argues that Jesus is God
He argues that Jesus was only a myth
He does not believe himself, yet argues that Jesus really existed
quiz.e: “Existence” and “deity” are two separate questions. The historical method can handle the first; the second calls for further inquiry and a personal response.

units.title: Are the Gospels Reliable?
units.sub: Four accounts do not match in every detail, and some people stop believing because of it. But investigators know that word-for-word identical statements are the suspicious ones.

share.v: but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

blocks.h: If four eyewitnesses gave statements about the same car accident and every word matched, the police would first suspect they had compared notes.

The four Gospels are exactly the opposite. Matthew says that when the synagogue leader came to Jesus, his daughter “has just died”; Mark records that she was “at the point of death.” Differences like these have led some people to lay down their faith, and have led others to ask more seriously: what kind of literature is this, really?

Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.
A distance of forty to sixty years

The estimate common in critical scholarship is this: Mark around AD 70, Matthew and Luke around AD 80–85, and John around AD 90–95. This is Bart Ehrman’s summary, and it is close to the mainstream view. Some Christian scholars, such as William Lane Craig, argue for earlier dates and think Luke may have been written in the AD 50s. Both sides admit that between Jesus’ death and the first Gospel lie several decades.
How was the story passed on during that gap? That is exactly the center of the debate.

At the Lunar New Year’s Eve reunion dinner, Uncle tells once again the story of how the whole family fled as refugees. Each year the wording differs a little, and sometimes there is an extra joke. But if he gets the year of the escape wrong, Grandma puts down her chopsticks at once and corrects him. The skeleton of the story has someone guarding it, and the details have room to breathe. This is exactly what scholars argue about: is the story of Jesus more like a reunion-dinner story with Grandma watching, or like the game of telephone that drifts further the more it is passed along?

In terms of genre, the Gospels are not modern biographies either. After comparing Greco-Roman biographies, Richard Burridge argues that the Gospels belong to this ancient genre. An ancient biography had to be faithful to its subject, but it did not record words verbatim the way a courtroom transcript does today.
Eyewitnesses, or collective memory?
Three views are set side by side below.

items.n: Bauckham: the Gospels stay close to eyewitness testimony
items.h: In Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, Richard Bauckham argues that the Synoptic Gospels stay quite close to the testimony of eyewitnesses, and that the Gospel of John comes from an eyewitness whom he identifies as John the Elder. The tradition did not drift and change inside anonymous communities; named witnesses were still alive and could be checked.

items.n: Ehrman: stories changed in the telling
items.h: In Jesus Before the Gospels, Ehrman draws on memory research to argue that the stories were remembered, altered and even created before they were written down; he holds that the Gospel authors were not eyewitnesses and had no access to eyewitnesses. The two men debated publicly in 2016, with respect for each other and opposite conclusions.

items.n: A middle path: a controlled tradition
items.h: Birger Gerhardsson, taking rabbinic teaching as his model, argues for a formal transmission by memorization; Kenneth Bailey, drawing on Middle Eastern village life, proposes an “informal but controlled” tradition guarded by the community together. Critics ask whether these models can be carried straight back to the first century.

blocks.h: One argument that has drawn attention concerns personal names. Bauckham compared the names in the Gospels and Acts with the data on Palestinian Jewish names collected by Tal Ilan and found that the distribution matches. For common names such as Simon and Joseph, the Gospels often add a note to tell them apart: “Simon Peter,” “Simon of Cyrene.” In 2023, Kamil Gregor and Brian Blais answered with a statistical test, arguing that this phenomenon is no better than the explanation of anonymous transmission; Luuk van de Weghe and Jason Wilson replied that their test was flawed and that the distribution of names fits the historical sources better than it fits fiction. The discussion has not been settled.
How should we view the differences?

Matthew says the centurion came forward himself to ask Jesus, while Luke says he sent elders and friends. Michael Licona compared Plutarch’s biographies and notes that ancient writers often used techniques such as compression, displacement and spotlighting, and he argues that the Gospels do something similar. His fellow evangelical Mark Strauss, in a review, largely affirmed him while admitting that some will feel he goes too far, because it touches on how inerrancy is defined. The traditional harmonizing reading and the literary-technique reading are both held within evangelicalism, and no verdict is given here.

Early testimony also has to be handled carefully. Papias, around AD 110, records that Mark wrote down Peter’s teaching from memory. Ehrman thinks Papias is almost entirely unreliable; other scholars think he deserves serious attention. The earliest fragment of John, P52, is also often said to date to “AD 125,” but papyrological studies actually give a wider range: Orsini and Clarysse suggest AD 125–175, and Brent Nongbri argues that the range should be extended into the late second century and even the early third. In preaching, do not present it as iron-clad proof.
Let us look separately at what is certain, what is disputed, and what is an inference of faith.

There really are differences in detail among the Gospels, for example the synagogue leader’s daughter and the way the centurion approached Jesus. Those who acknowledge these differences include evangelical scholars themselves.
The mainstream estimate puts Mark around AD 70 and John around AD 90–95; those who argue for earlier dates are a minority, but they do exist.
Most scholars treat the Gospels as a genre close to Greco-Roman biography; this cannot by itself settle the historicity of each detail.

How close the Gospels stand to the eyewitnesses is still debated among scholars. Bauckham and Ehrman hold nearly opposite positions, and the statistical significance of the names argument is still being contested.
The date of P52 cannot be pinned down to a single year. The second century is the usual judgment, but the upper and lower limits are still disputed.

The Gospels preserve the true testimony needed to know Jesus, and God’s Spirit uses it. This is trust based on evidence and also a judgment of faith; the historical method by itself cannot draw this conclusion.
He entrusted life to testimony

God could have dropped a sealed book down from heaven. Instead He chose to let fishermen, a tax collector and a doctor who investigated with care leave their testimony, and He kept even their different angles. This God is not afraid of being examined.

Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

The Gospels also keep many passages that the authors themselves would never want to invent: in His hometown Jesus “could do no mighty work,” and Peter denied his Lord three times. All of this testimony finally leads to the same place: the cross and the empty tomb. This is the very core of the early message that Paul preserved in his own writing.

For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
Open to Mark chapter 2 and read it slowly once through. Imagine you are among the first to hear this story, and notice which details the author did not need to include but did.
Meditate: When I read the Gospels, is it to find fault, to finish my reading plan, or to meet the living Lord?

Pray: Faithful Lord, thank You that I can come to know You through these testimonies. When I have questions, I will bring them honestly before You; what I do not understand, give me patience. May I read not only words but meet the Jesus who died and rose for me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: A standard has to be read well before it can be used. This week, read Mark as a book from start to finish, without turning to the notes first.

Humility overcomes pride: There is no need to exaggerate for the Bible, and no need to pretend there are no difficulties. Saying “I don’t know the answer to this one yet” is a better witness than forcing an answer.
Change your mindset, change your life: The purpose of reading the Gospels is to know Jesus, and to let that knowledge change how I respond to people and to events.

blocks.h: This week: Read the Gospel of Mark in one sitting (about two hours). Note one detail you never noticed and one question that puzzles you, and take them to a spiritual companion.
Pass it on: “Have you ever read a Gospel yourself from beginning to end? Would you read Mark all the way through and then tell me what you think?”
Quiz

quiz.q: What was the main point of disagreement in the 2016 debate between Ehrman and Bauckham?
o: Whether the Gospels are directly connected to eyewitness testimony
Whether Jesus really existed
Whether the Gospels were written in Greek
quiz.e: Both admit that Jesus existed; Bauckham argues that the Gospels stay close to the eyewitnesses, and Ehrman takes the opposite view.

quiz.q: How does Licona explain some of the differences among the Gospels?
o: They must be copyists’ mistakes
They are all fiction
Through techniques such as compression and displacement, common in ancient biography
quiz.e: This is his claim after comparing Plutarch. Evangelicals also hold different views on it.

quiz.q: What is the more honest statement about the P52 fragment?
o: It can be dated precisely to AD 125
Its date has a range and is disputed, so it should not be used as iron-clad proof
It has been proved to be in John’s own hand
quiz.e: The range given by papyrologists is wide, and that should be kept when citing it.

units.title: Who Did He Say He Was?
units.sub: One sentence, “Your sins are forgiven,” made the scribes in the corner decide He had blasphemed. Whom did He take Himself to be?

share.v: Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”

blocks.h: The roof is torn open, and a paralyzed man is let down on ropes before a carpenter. Everyone waits for Him to heal. Instead He opens His mouth and says something far more outrageous.

Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” But there were some of the scribes sitting there and reasoning in their hearts, “Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
The scribes understood the weight of that sentence. And that is what this whole unit asks: how did Jesus actually see Himself?
His favorite title: the Son of Man

In the Gospels, “Son of Man” comes almost only from Jesus’ own mouth. In Aramaic the phrase can mean simply “a person,” and so it sounds quite ordinary. But Daniel chapter 7 has one “like a son of man” who comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting authority. When Jesus stood trial before the high priest, Mark records that He applied exactly this picture to Himself.

I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him near before him. Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom one that will not be destroyed.
Forgiving sins, the Sabbath and “I AM”

A convenience store clerk looks up while ringing you out and says, “Your mortgage? I’ve canceled it for you.” You can only have two reactions: this person has a problem, or he owns the bank. Forgiving the debt people owe to God is that kind of statement.
Jesus also said that “the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” The Sabbath is a commandment God Himself established, and calling oneself its lord means standing on the lawgiver’s side.

The declaration in John is more direct still: “before Abraham came into existence, I AM.” This “I AM” (Greek ego eimi) calls to mind what God said to Moses in the burning bush. The listeners of the day picked up stones, and their reason is written out plainly: “you, being a man, make yourself God.”
What scholars say
Historians do not necessarily regard every word in the Gospels as spoken by Jesus Himself, and that is exactly where the debate lies.

items.h: Bart Ehrman argues that the historical Jesus did not call Himself God and that sayings such as “I and the Father are one” come from later developments; he thinks the Son of Man in Jesus’ mouth was another figure still to come. He also admits that soon after Jesus’ death the disciples believed He had been exalted to divine status. He writes as a historian, not as a Christian.

Larry Hurtado approaches the question through liturgy and worship: devotion to Jesus appeared very early, in varied and fervent forms, and yet the believers still saw themselves as Jewish monotheists. This was not something that seeped in during the late Hellenistic period.

Richard Bauckham argues that the New Testament writers include Jesus within the identity of the one God of Israel; for example, Philippians 2 applies to Jesus the words of Isaiah, “to me every knee shall bow.”

items.n: Boyarin: another line from the Jewish background
items.h: The Jewish scholar Daniel Boyarin argues that the Son of Man is a divine figure drawn from Daniel 7, and that this expectation already existed in Judaism at the time. He is not a Christian, and some scholars consider his view an overreach.

blocks.h: The strength and limits of “Lunatic, Liar or Lord”

C. S. Lewis popularized this argument in Mere Christianity (1952): a man who said these things could not be merely a great moral teacher; he was either a lunatic, or the Devil, or God. The form has predecessors, such as Henry Liddon in the nineteenth century. Critics point to its weakness: it presupposes that Jesus really said these things. John Hick and Ehrman both think that Jesus’ own claim to be God is not an established historical conclusion, and even the Christian philosopher William Lane Craig cautions that “legend” should be added as a fourth possibility. So the argument stands only when combined with the Gospel sources (the previous unit), and used alone it is not enough.

A firmer path is to look at the material that even skeptical scholars find harder to assign to later theology: the authority with which Jesus acted, His being charged with blasphemy and executed, and the early worship already preserved in Paul’s letters. As for the “I AM” sayings in John, many scholars regard them as an expression of deepened theology, while Christians believe they faithfully convey who Jesus was; the disagreement also involves one’s judgment about the genre of John.
Let us take it in layers: what is a fact about the text, what is a historical dispute, and what is a confession of faith.

The Gospels record Jesus calling Himself the Son of Man, forgiving sins and calling Himself lord of the Sabbath. This is what the text says and is not in dispute. Whether each saying came from the lips of the historical Jesus is another matter.

Devotion to Jesus appeared very early and can already be seen in Paul’s letters. Ehrman also agrees that belief in Jesus’ divinity arose soon after His death; the disagreement is over what kind of belief it was.

To what extent did the historical Jesus openly claim to be God? Scholarly opinion is divided. Ehrman and Hick deny it; Bauckham, Michael Bird and others think the early high Christology has roots in Jesus Himself.
Was the Son of Man already a recognized divine figure in the Second Temple period? Boyarin argues so, while Ehrman holds that the Son of Man in Daniel symbolizes Israel; the matter is unsettled.
Jesus is truly God become flesh. Lewis’ trilemma forcefully reminds us that “good teacher” is not a stable conclusion, but it is not a logical proof. This is a confession of faith.
The One who says “I AM” went to the cross
Put these declarations side by side, and the most surprising thing is the way He exercised His authority. The One worthy of every knee bowing knelt to wash feet and walked to the cross.

who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

This passage echoes Isaiah, where God declares His sole sovereignty. The New Testament writers dared to apply those words to a man who had been crucified. His authority to forgive sins was finally paid for with His own blood.
I have sworn by myself. The word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not be revoked, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
Read Mark 2:1-12 and put yourself in the place of the paralyzed man: your friends have carried you to Him, and He looks at you and says, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” Stay there for a minute.
Meditate: Where in my heart have I placed Jesus? As a good teacher, a helper who solves my problems, or the Lord before whom I bow my knee?

Pray: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often only want to use You and am unwilling to obey You. You are worthy of every knee bowing, yet for me You took the form of a servant and went to the cross. Reign in my life, forgive my sins, and let my tongue sincerely confess that You are Lord. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus reign: If He really is the One He declared Himself to be, He cannot be only an advisor. Choose one area where you have always been the one in charge and hand it over to Him.
Letting God be God and people be people: He has the authority to forgive sins; I have no right to judge. Step down from the seat of condemning others.
Jesus is my example: The One with the highest authority chose to empty Himself. Today use whatever small authority you have to serve one person.

blocks.h: This week: Finish reading Mark 2 and Philippians 2, and write one sentence: “If Jesus is Lord, the one thing I will change this week is…” Then tell a spiritual companion.
Pass it on: “Many people say Jesus was a good teacher. But if a teacher said to you, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ what would you make of him?”
Quiz

quiz.q: Why did the scribes think Jesus was “speaking blasphemies”?
o: Because He healed the sick
Because He preached on the Sabbath
Because He forgave sins, which they believed only God can do
quiz.e: Mark 2:7: Who can forgive sins but God alone?

quiz.q: Which statement is closest to Ehrman’s view of Jesus’ self-claims?
o: The historical Jesus did not call Himself God, and belief in His divinity arose after His death
He believes Jesus personally declared Himself to be God
Jesus never existed
quiz.e: He believes Jesus existed and agrees that the belief arose early, but he does not think Jesus claimed to be God. When citing him, stay faithful to his position.

quiz.q: What is the main limitation of Lewis’ trilemma?
o: Lewis was not a Christian
It presupposes that Jesus really said these things, and so needs support from the historical sources
It is the latest scientific discovery
quiz.e: Critics raise the possibility of legend, so it must be used together with an examination of the Gospel sources.

units.title: Miracles: Were the Laws of Nature Broken?
units.sub: When money goes missing from your drawer, you do not report that mathematics is broken. The debate over miracles is more interesting than most people think, and harder.

share.v: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.

blocks.h: Put two bills in a drawer, and the next day only one is left. You would suspect that someone has been into the drawer. You would not suspect that one plus one no longer equals two.
C. S. Lewis used a similar example to ask a question: when a miracle happens, what exactly is it that gets broken? The people in the Gospels were asking a different question.

He awoke and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind ceased and there was a great calm. He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?” They were greatly afraid and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
The door Hume closed

In 1748 the Scottish philosopher David Hume published “Of Miracles.” He defined a miracle as a violation of the laws of nature. The laws of nature come from humanity’s uniform experience, so the evidence against miracles is as strong as evidence can be; unless the falsehood of the testimony would be more miraculous than the miracle itself, we should not believe. He also pointed out that testimony to miracles is often mixed with fanaticism and self-interest, and that the miracle reports of the various religions cancel one another out.
Some of these cautions remain valid today. Swindlers really do use miracles to make money, and people really do remember coincidences as wonders.
How tightly is the door shut?

On a billiard table, the laws of physics can calculate the path of the cue ball after it strikes the red ball. But if you reach out halfway and pick up the red ball, are the laws broken? The laws keep working as usual; there is only an extra hand. They tell you what will happen “when no outside force intervenes”; they do not guarantee that there is no hand.

This is the line of thought in Lewis’ Miracles (1947): the laws of nature are regularities, and a miracle is a new event added from outside nature. Critics reply that this requires first admitting that there is such a hand. So the heart of the matter is really upstream: do you believe in God?

The philosopher of science John Earman, in Hume’s Abject Failure (2000), argued that Hume’s argument fails in probability theory: enough independent testimonies can, in principle, outweigh a very low prior probability. He is criticizing Hume’s logic, not defending Christianity; and some Hume scholars have replied to him, saying he did not read Hume within the whole of his thought.
Can history speak about miracles?
This is another door, and there are three main answers.

items.n: Ehrman: not possible, as a matter of method
items.h: Bart Ehrman argues that history can only establish “what probably happened,” and a miracle by definition is the least probable thing, so historians cannot prove that a miracle occurred. He says this is a problem of method, and he does not claim that miracles can never exist.

Michael Licona replies that to say a miracle is impossible, one needs background knowledge that God is unlikely to exist or to act. Historians should lay their worldviews on the table, not use method to rule out the conclusion in advance.

items.n: Keener: at least hear the witnesses
items.h: In his two-volume, 1,172-page Miracles, Craig Keener collects contemporary testimonies to miracles from around the world, arguing that they are not proof but are evidence, and should not be excluded before one even walks in the door. He also admits that not every case is supernatural.

blocks.h: What does the research say? Hear the bad news too

The STEP trial of 2006 randomly assigned 1,802 heart bypass surgery patients: among those who did not know whether they were being prayed for, those prayed for and those not prayed for showed no significant difference in complications; the group who knew for certain that people were praying for them actually had slightly more complications (59% versus 51%). A 2009 Cochrane review also concluded that most studies showed no effect, while the overall evidence was inconclusive, neither supporting nor opposing prayer. On the other hand, in 2010 Brown (Candy Gunther Brown) and colleagues studied face-to-face prayer with the laying on of hands in Mozambique, and the hearing and vision measurements of 24 subjects improved; but there was no control group and the sample was very small, so expectation and other factors cannot be ruled out.

How might a Christian view this? A clinical trial can measure a protocol of human intercession, but it can hardly “test” a personal God who responds freely. That is a reasonable caution, and it can also turn into an excuse that can never be tested. Both sides need to be admitted honestly. Hume’s other warning also remains: other religions have miracle reports too. Keener’s answer is to judge case by case, and some may be natural causes or even fraud. The reviewer Hughson Ong thinks his rebuttal of atheism does not go deep enough.
Philosophy, history and clinical research need to be looked at separately.
Hume’s “Of Miracles” (1748) defines a miracle as a violation of the laws of nature and is still the starting point of the discussion.

The large randomized trial STEP found no improvement in surgical outcomes from distant intercessory prayer; the group who knew for certain that people were praying for them had slightly more complications. Most studies in the Cochrane review also showed no effect, and its overall conclusion was that the evidence is inconclusive.
The first part of Hume’s argument has received a strong probabilistic critique from Earman and others, and some have defended Hume; the discussion continues.

Contemporary miracle testimonies (Keener) and studies of face-to-face prayer (Brown) both offer material worth examining, but the samples, controls and degree of verification are limited, and they do not amount to proof.
Can history judge that a miracle has occurred? Ehrman says no and Licona says yes; the core of the dispute is worldview presuppositions.
If there is a God who created and sustains nature, miracles are not logically contrary to reason. That the miracles of Jesus are real is a judgment of faith based on the testimony of the Gospels.
The One the signs point to
The Gospel of John does not much use the word “wonders”; it mostly calls them “signs.” A sign wants you to look up and see where it points.
This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

John the Baptist began to doubt in prison and sent people to ask. Jesus answered him with Isaiah’s hope, and every item is restoration: seeing, walking, hearing. His power always turns toward human brokenness and is never for show.

Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.

But John was never rescued from prison in the end. Paul’s thorn was never taken away. The greatest sign is that Jesus Himself did not come down from the cross, and on the third day came out of the tomb. So those today who have not been healed are not excluded from this grace; what they wait for is the final redemption of the body.
He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.
Think of someone you have prayed for who has still not been healed; it may be you yourself. There is no need to hurry to explain. Say that name slowly to the Lord.
Meditate: Do I want the miracle, or the Lord who works miracles? If He does not do what I asked this time, am I still willing to pour out my heart to Him?

Pray: Lord Jesus, You could calm the wind and the sea, and on the cross You also went through the night of not being rescued. I bring my sickness and my waiting to You, and I ask You to heal; my faith is small, so help me. Give me grace that is sufficient, and strengthen my hope of the resurrection. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Letting God be God: You may ask boldly, but do not manipulate God, write checks on His behalf, or tell a sick person, “It’s because your faith is not enough.”

The Holy Spirit is my guide: When praying for the sick, first ask the Holy Spirit: should I speak, or simply keep them company? Asking God for healing and seeing a doctor do not conflict; for persistent symptoms, please seek medical care.
God’s eternal perspective: The greatest healing is complete only on the day of resurrection; today’s grace is enough for today’s road.

blocks.h: This week: Visit or check in on someone who has been ill for a long time. Offer no advice; ask only, “How can I pray for you?” and then really pray for them.
Pass it on: “Have you ever come across something you still cannot explain? What would you need to see before you would believe there is power beyond nature?”
Quiz

quiz.q: What is the main point of Earman’s criticism of Hume?
o: His probabilistic reasoning is flawed, and enough independent testimonies can in principle overcome low probability
He had seen a miracle with his own eyes
He proved Christianity to be true
quiz.e: Earman criticizes Hume’s logic; he is not defending Christianity.

quiz.q: What was the result of the 2006 STEP study of intercessory prayer?
o: Intercessory prayer greatly reduced complications
Distant intercessory prayer did not improve surgical outcomes
The study proved that God does not exist
quiz.e: Face it honestly: it measured only a particular protocol of intercessory prayer, and it neither proves that God does not exist nor supports treating prayer as a therapy.

quiz.q: What word does the Gospel of John mostly use for the miracles of Jesus?
o: Magic
Natural phenomena
Signs
quiz.e: A sign points to who Jesus is; its purpose is not display.

units.title: The Sermon on the Mount: Teaching That Turns the World Upside Down
units.sub: A teaching you can read in a dozen minutes made an Indian lawyer, a German pastor and an American pastor rethink how to face their enemies.

share.v: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.

blocks.h: A Hindu lawyer who was never baptized read Matthew chapters five to seven as a young man in London, and later wrote in his autobiography that the passage went straight to his heart. An African American pastor, leading a civil rights movement under bomb threats, said he had walked back to this teaching. A German pastor wrote a book on it in the Nazi era and later died on the gallows in a concentration camp.

These three men are Gandhi, King and Bonhoeffer. What links them is a teaching that takes only about a dozen minutes to read from beginning to end. Its very first sentence turns the world’s ranking of success upside down.
Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
There are no winners on the list of the blessed

The Beatitudes list the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness. Submit that as a job application and it would mostly fail the first screening. Yet Jesus says these are the blessed ones.

The Greek word for “blessed,” makarios, is hard to translate with a single word. The New Testament scholar Jonathan Pennington argues that the Beatitudes portray what real flourishing looks like for people centered on God: a picture of a life, not a checklist for “do these and collect your prize.”

Ordinary life is like climbing a ladder: the higher you go, the more blessed you are. Jesus’ list lays the ladder down and turns it into a bridge. The first to walk across are those who admit they cannot climb.
From the deed in the hand to the motive in the heart

Six times the pattern “You have heard that it was said… but I tell you” chases the law from behavior into the heart: not only do not murder, but deal with anger; not only do not commit adultery, but deal with the eyes. Even doing good, praying and fasting must face a question: for whom am I doing this?

But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.

In Stride Toward Freedom, recalling the Montgomery bus boycott, King said that Christ furnished the spirit and the motivation while Gandhi furnished the method. Gandhi, for his part, wrote in his autobiography about the impact the Sermon on the Mount had on him, and set it beside the Bhagavad Gita. He never became a Christian.

A saying attributed to Gandhi circulates online: “I like your Christ, I do not like your Christians.” We cannot find a reliable first-hand source, so we do not quote it. The genuine record is strong enough that it needs no help from a saying of unknown origin.
How distinctive is this teaching?

To be honest, much of the content was not heard first here. Confucius said not to do to others what you would not want done to yourself; the Jewish rabbi Hillel summed up the Law as not doing to your fellow what you hate. The philosopher Marcus Singer points out that the difference between the negative and positive forms is often exaggerated. Bertrand Russell also noted that Lao Tzu and the Buddha had already taught principles such as repaying evil with good. Christians need not deny any of this, for rays of goodness have always been scattered among people.

What is truly unusual is where the speaker places Himself: “But I tell you,” and He even says that whether one stands or falls depends on how one treats “these words of mine.” This is exactly what astonished the listeners.
When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.

The sharpest objection comes from Nietzsche. In On the Genealogy of Morality (1887) he argued that virtues such as gentleness and not taking revenge are really the weak dressing up their inability to strike back as morality. This criticism deserves a hearing, because some people do use “forgiveness” to cover cowardice. But when Jesus speaks of gentleness, He holds the choice in His hands, and King and Bonhoeffer also took this road only after counting the cost. Which of the two accounts is right depends on lives, and on what you believe the ultimate nature of the universe to be.
A sermon arranged by Matthew’s own hand?

Luke 6 has a shorter “Sermon on the Plain,” about a quarter the length of the Sermon on the Mount; material such as the Lord’s Prayer appears elsewhere in Luke. Many scholars therefore think Matthew compiled Jesus’ teachings into this sermon and did not record a single day’s speech word for word. Others think Jesus must have taught similar content many times on different occasions. Neither view denies that these teachings come from Jesus.

How to live out this passage has been argued over by the church for two thousand years. Tolstoy (1894) took it as a literal command of non-resistance; several main readings are set side by side below.

items.h: The Anabaptist tradition and Tolstoy: Christians should not swear oaths, take revenge or use force, and this is precisely the church’s witness.
Luther: you may endure wrong done to yourself, but as a judge or a parent you have a duty to protect others.

Many contemporary evangelical scholars: this is a way of life that the citizens of the kingdom begin to live now and that will be fully realized when the Lord returns, learned step by step through the Holy Spirit.

blocks.h: Let us take each claim separately and mark how certain it is.
Gandhi said in his autobiography that the Sermon on the Mount went straight to his heart, but he never became a Christian.
King stated plainly that Christ furnished the spirit and motivation and Gandhi furnished the method. He also said that he went back to the Sermon on the Mount and to Gandhi’s method of nonviolence.

Bonhoeffer’s Discipleship (Nachfolge) was published in 1937 and centers on an exposition of the Sermon on the Mount. He was arrested in 1943 for his involvement in the plot against Hitler and died at Flossenbürg on April 9, 1945.
That the Sermon on the Mount was compiled by Matthew from Jesus’ teachings is the view of most scholars, but the specific sources (such as the Q document) remain a hypothesis.
Whether makarios is best understood as “flourishing” or as “blessed” is still discussed among scholars.

Gentleness and love of enemies are true strength and not a self-consolation of the weak. This is a judgment of theology and values; history can supply witnesses, but it cannot decide the matter by itself.
This standard brings us to grace

Reading “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect,” any honest person feels a sinking in the heart. If this were the exam paper for getting into heaven, no one would pass.
for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,

That is why the first sentence matters so much: the kingdom of heaven belongs to the “poor in spirit,” those who know they come with empty hands. Here the law is like a mirror that shows us we need a Savior. Grace comes first, and then obedience has roots.
Jesus walked this road Himself. He told His disciples to pray for those who persecute them, and on the cross He prayed this very prayer:
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots.
Loving enemies is not only His teaching; it is how God treats us. We once stood on the side of hostility, and He reached out His hand first:
For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.

Here God’s righteousness and goodness meet. His standard has not been lowered by a single point, yet His Son paid the price for us and put new life within us, so that we begin to learn to live this way.
Read the Beatitudes slowly once, pausing three seconds after each line, and ask yourself: which of these lines do I lack the most? Circle it.
Meditate: Lately, have I done a good deed so that others would see it? Is there a person whose memory makes my chest tighten?

Pray: Father in heaven, I confess that I cannot live out this teaching on my own. Forgive my pride and my anger, give me a poor spirit, and give me grace to pray for the one who hurt me. If I am in danger now, lead me to safety and help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: The Sermon on the Mount is not a motto to hang on the wall. Choosing one verse each week to live out is more useful than memorizing the whole.

Humility overcomes pride: Being “poor in spirit” is the starting point. The self-centered are in a hurry to prove themselves; the selfless can leave the credit with God and feel at ease doing good in secret.
People matter more than tasks: Before arguing about who is right, deal with the relationship. Jesus said to go first and be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

blocks.h: Please note: “Turn the other cheek” teaches letting go of revenge; it does not require anyone to stay in the midst of violence. When Jesus Himself was struck, He questioned the one who struck Him (John 18:22-23). If you are suffering domestic violence or abuse, seeking safety and professional help is right; please contact your local protection hotline and people you trust.

This week: Write down the name of one person who troubles you, and for seven days in a row pray one sentence for them, asking not that they change but only that God would bless them. If this person has seriously hurt you, you may begin by giving the pain to God, and you need not force more.
Pass it on: Do you think “love your enemies” is real strength, or too impractical? Have you ever met someone who really lived this way?
Quiz

quiz.q: How did King describe the influence of Jesus and Gandhi on him?
o: Christ furnished the spirit and motivation, Gandhi furnished the method
The two teachings were exactly the same
Gandhi led him to be baptized into Christ
quiz.e: King said this himself. Gandhi, for his part, never became a Christian.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the relation of the Sermon on the Mount to the moral teaching of other cultures?
o: Other cultures never had similar teachings
Jesus copied Confucius
The Golden Rule and other lights of goodness exist elsewhere; what is unusual about Jesus is that He speaks on His own authority
quiz.e: Christians need not deny the light found elsewhere; what astonished the listeners is that He taught “with authority.”

quiz.q: What does “turn the other cheek” mean for a victim of domestic violence?
o: They must endure and stay where they are
Do not take revenge, but it is right to seek safety and professional help
They must forgive first before they may ask for help
quiz.e: The saying addresses the heart of revenge; it does not ask anyone to remain in violence. When Jesus was struck, He questioned the one who struck Him.

units.title: A Flawless Character
units.sub: He asked in public, “Which of you convicts me of sin?” An English philosopher actually stepped forward and answered.

share.v: Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?

blocks.h: When you get home tonight, ask the person closest to you one question: “Can you point out what is wrong with me?” Then brew a pot of tea, because the answer will be long.
The Gospels record a man who asked this question of a crowd of opponents who were looking for something to seize on.
Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?
This sentence is either arrogance or honesty. Today we lay out His record, and we invite the harshest critics to look at it with us.
The people He stopped for

In the Gospels, Jesus’ day is constantly being interrupted: children brought to be touched, a tax collector up a tree, a woman weeping at a dinner party. The disciples and the host saw all of these as distractions, but He stopped.

The law required a person with leprosy to live alone outside the camp and to call out from a distance, “Unclean!” Mark records Jesus’ reaction: “Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him.” Scholars remind us that the “leprosy” here probably refers broadly to skin diseases and is not necessarily Hansen’s disease as we know it today; the heart of the problem was ritual uncleanness. He could have healed with a single word, but first He stretched out His hand.

A white shirt that touches a stain gets stained; bleach that touches a stain makes the stain retreat. People of that time feared that uncleanness was contagious. In the Gospels, when Jesus touches an unclean person, the contagion runs in the opposite direction.

He went to dine at Zacchaeus’ house, while the crowd murmured, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” He spoke with a Samaritan woman, which astonished even His disciples. Luke also records several women who traveled with Him and supported Jesus and the disciples out of their own means.
He gets angry too

Flawless does not mean lukewarm. Mark says that in the synagogue Jesus “looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts,” because some people would rather keep the rules than see a withered hand restored. When the disciples tried to keep the children away, He too was “moved with indignation.” His anger was almost always directed at those who kept people out, and seldom at anything for the sake of His own face.
Russell’s three charges

On March 6, 1927, the philosopher Bertrand Russell gave a lecture at Battersea Town Hall in London, “Why I Am Not a Christian.” He began by affirming teachings of Jesus such as turning the other cheek, and then he objected. First, a truly compassionate person would not believe in eternal punishment, and he called the doctrine of hell a doctrine of cruelty. Second, sending demons into a herd of pigs was unfair to the pigs. Third, the fig tree was cursed when it was not the season for figs, so what had the tree done wrong? His conclusion was that for wisdom and virtue he would rank the Buddha and Socrates above Jesus.
These criticisms deserve a direct answer and should not be passed over as a joke. The first is the weightiest, and the views are laid out separately below.

items.h: Hell is eternal punishment for those who reject God. Defenders say that if God’s justice did not judge evil, the tears of the victims would have been shed for nothing; Jesus Himself spoke of judgment many times, and wept over the city that would not turn back.

Some evangelical scholars also argue that unbelievers finally come to destruction and are not tormented forever. John Stott put this view forward cautiously in Essentials in 1988. A 2000 report of the Evangelical Alliance in the UK called it a clear minority opinion among evangelicals.

Whatever the details, a teacher who threatens his hearers with eternal fire is morally inferior to Socrates, who faced his opponents calmly. This intuition moves many people, and it is a problem Christians should face honestly.

blocks.h: As for the fig tree, most interpreters read it as a prophetic sign-act: Mark sandwiches it around the cleansing of the temple, and its point is aimed at a religion with leaves but no fruit. This reading has a basis in the text, but if you still feel uneasy after reading it, there is no need to hurry to suppress that unease.
Do not step into another pit

When speaking of how Jesus treated women, Christians often paint the Judaism of the time as unrelieved darkness to set Jesus off. The Jewish New Testament scholar Amy-Jill Levine, in The Misunderstood Jew, points out that this is a stereotype. Jesus Himself was a Jew, and His compassion has roots in the Jewish tradition. Praising Jesus does not require first putting down His own people.

The hardest passage is Mark 7:27, where Jesus says to a Gentile mother, “it is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Some scholars say plainly that this is an insult. N. Clayton Croy, in New Testament Studies in 2024, argues that the diminutive in the original is closer to “little dogs” and that the point is the order of Jewish priority; and the woman answered cleverly, and He gave way on the spot to her words. Scholars remain divided on this.

How do historians see His influence? The nineteenth-century Irish historian W. E. H. Lecky was quite critical of church history, yet in his History of European Morals he wrote that “the simple record of three short years of active life” has done more to regenerate and soften mankind than all the writings of philosophers and the exhortations of moralists. This is an assessment of influence; it does not mean he accepted the doctrine that Jesus was sinless.
The subject of character slides most easily into hymn-singing, so we take it in layers.
Russell’s 1927 lecture really did criticize Jesus’ teaching on hell and the accounts of the pigs and the fig tree, and ranked the Buddha and Socrates above Him.

The Gospels present Jesus as close to people regarded at the time as unclean or sinful. This main line is solid; how startling these acts were in the first-century Jewish setting is still discussed by scholars, and it should not be simplified into Jesus against Judaism.
Whether Mark 7:27 carries a tone of insult is viewed differently by scholars.
The nature of hell is understood in different ways within evangelicalism; traditional eternal punishment is still the majority view, and conditional immortality is a clear minority.

“Jesus was sinless” is not a conclusion history can verify. The sources were written by people who loved Him, and no one can verify a person’s inner heart. The New Testament’s declaration is a witness of faith (1 Peter is traditionally attributed to Peter, though the question of authorship is also discussed among scholars), and all we can check is whether that witness fits the record He left.
For whom does such a character live?

The first people to declare Jesus sinless were the very ones who ate with Him, argued with Him and walked with Him the most. They even recorded that He was hungry, tired and wept. Peter had seen Him on trial with his own eyes and with his own mouth had denied Him.
who didn’t sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.” When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.
His goodness does not hang in midair. The New Testament says He was truly tempted, and so He understands your struggles and mine.
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.

If the story stopped here, Jesus would be only a ruler against which we measure ourselves, and having measured, we would be even more despairing. The New Testament goes further: this flawless One put Himself in the place where we should stand. His character is the premise of the cross, and the cross is the purpose of His character.
For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
Read Mark 1:40-42 slowly, and pause at “touched him.” Think about which part of you is the part you assume He would not want to touch.
Meditate: When I am angry today, is it because someone is being kept outside the door, or because of my own face?

Pray: Lord Jesus, You stopped to see the ones people passed over, and You saw me. My goodness cannot last through a single meal, yet You were made sin for me. Forgive me, and change me by Your Spirit, so that I treat people the way You treat me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: Begin not with His great doctrines but with His stopping on the road. Whoever is interrupting me today may be exactly the person I am meant to see.
People matter more than tasks: On His way to save Jairus’ daughter, He still stopped for a woman. My schedule is not the master of my life.
Humility overcomes pride: My anger is mostly about myself. Ask God to help me see this clearly, and be the first to admit fault to the one I have hurt.

blocks.h: This week: Find one person you see every day but have never really looked at, such as a security guard, a cleaning lady or a colleague’s assistant. Ask for their name, remember it, and call them by it next time.
Pass it on: “In the stories about Jesus that you have heard, is there anything that made you feel He did something not quite right? I would really like to hear it.”
Quiz

quiz.q: What was the heaviest moral criticism of Jesus in Russell’s 1927 lecture?
o: He was not learned enough
He taught eternal punishment
He left no writings
quiz.e: Russell held that a truly compassionate person would not believe in eternal punishment, and he also mentioned the pigs and the fig tree.

quiz.q: What does Levine remind Christians to avoid when speaking of how Jesus treated women?
o: Painting the Judaism of the time as unrelieved darkness to set Jesus off
Mentioning the women in the Gospels
Quoting the Gospel of Mark
quiz.e: Praising Jesus does not require putting down His fellow Jews.

quiz.q: Why is “Jesus was sinless” a declaration of faith and not a historical conclusion?
o: Because the sources have all been lost
Because the Gospels deny it
Because history cannot verify a person’s inner heart, and the sources come from his followers
quiz.e: What we can check is whether the witness fits the record; sinlessness cannot be proved by historical method.

units.title: The Cross: Why Did He Have to Die?
units.sub: Romans would not even say the word. Christians put it on their rooftops.

share.v: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

blocks.h: Picture a church with a gallows standing on its roof, and a bride wearing a tiny golden noose around her neck. You would think these people had lost their minds.

On the Palatine Hill in imperial Rome, someone scratched a graffito into the wall plaster: a man with a donkey’s head hanging on a cross, another figure beside him with a hand raised, and a line of Greek reading “Alexamenos worships his god.” It is generally taken as a mockery of a Christian, and is most often dated somewhere between the second and third centuries. To people then, worshiping a man who had been nailed to a cross was that ridiculous.
For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
The word Romans would not say

In the first century BC the Roman statesman Cicero prosecuted Verres, the governor of Sicily, for crucifying a man who kept crying out, “I am a Roman citizen,” and called this punishment the most cruel and terrible. In another speech he argued that even the name of the cross should stay far away not only from the body of a Roman citizen but from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears.

Martin Hengel’s classic little book of 1977 gathers the evidence for how widely this punishment was used in the ancient world. It fell mostly on the lower classes and slaves, was carried out in public places, and was meant to deter. Ancient writers rarely criticized it.

Suppose someone told you today that his savior died in the electric chair, and was clearly guilty besides. What would be your first reaction? A first-century listener who heard about “Christ crucified” probably felt the same thing, only more revulsion.
A nail in the bone

In 1968 archaeologists found the remains of a first-century man in a tomb northeast of Jerusalem. His name was Yehohanan, and an iron nail was still lodged in his heel bone. The early reports were later revised: scholars have reassessed the length of the nail, whether the arms were nailed, and whether the leg bones were broken. The bones have since been reburied, so today they can only be studied from photographs and models.

Physical evidence remains very scarce. Researchers gave a calcaneal injury on a skeleton from Gavello, Italy, the cautious title of a “possible” case, and in 2017 a man with a nail through his heel was found at Fenstanton in England, dated to roughly AD 130 to 360.
Who killed Him?

The historical answer is fairly clear: the Roman governor Pilate gave the order, and the charge was “the King of the Jews.” To Rome that was a political crime. The Roman historian Tacitus also records that Christ was put to death by Pilate during the reign of Tiberius. The Gospels also record that some of the religious leaders of the time took part.
The superscription of his accusation was written over him: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

Some in history have used this to lay the guilt on the whole Jewish people, and it has done enormous harm. That is wrong, and Christians should plainly reject it. Jesus Himself was a Jew, and the Bible says, “All we like sheep have gone astray,” which puts every one of us inside this event.
Why did He have to die?

The New Testament uses many pictures, like photographs of one mountain taken from different angles. In the early 1930s the Swedish theologian Gustaf Aulén grouped the church’s understandings into three main types. The evangelical tradition gives special weight to substitution, and it need not let go of the other aspects because of that.

items.h: What our sin deserved, Christ bore (Isaiah 53:5-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The question it answers: how can a righteous God forgive, rather than pretend nothing happened?
Through His death Christ defeated the powers of sin, death and darkness (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14-15). Aulén held that this was the church’s dominant way of speaking in its first thousand years.

items.n: Example and the moving power of love
items.h: The cross displays God’s love and moves people to turn back (1 John 4:9-10). It is often linked with Abelard in the Middle Ages; critics say that if this were the only side, being moved would not settle the debt of sin.
The cross tears down the walls between people and God, and between people and one another (Romans 3:25-26). This side often sits alongside the ones above.

blocks.h: “Cosmic child abuse”?

The sharpest criticism comes in two strands. In 1989 Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker criticized substitutionary theology from the standpoint of abuse survivors, arguing that it can lead people to glorify suffering. In 2003 the British evangelical pastor Steve Chalke and Alan Mann likewise wrote that if substitution is told as a vengeful Father punishing an innocent Son, it becomes “cosmic child abuse.”

Garry Williams’s response in 2007 pointed out that Jesus was an adult with a mature will, not a helpless child, and that the work of the Trinity is undivided, so sending and self-giving are two sides of one love. Still, the critics’ worry deserves to be heard: the church must never use the cross to tell abuse victims to stay in the violence.

A judge hands you a fine you cannot pay, then takes off his robe, steps down, and pays it for you. This picture shows how justice and mercy can both stand, but it has limits: the One on the cross was not a third party. The New Testament says “God was in Christ,” bearing it Himself.
Separate the historical facts from the theological interpretation.
Jesus was crucified under Pilate. Ancient sources, both Christian and non-Christian, support this.
Roman crucifixion was a public, shaming form of torture, and Cicero and others left records of their revulsion.

The 1968 remains of Yehohanan are the best-known physical evidence; the details of how he was nailed have been revised several times, and some uncertainty remains. The other cases (Gavello and Fenstanton) are more recent, and their interpretation is more cautious.
The Alexamenos graffito is generally read as a mockery of Christians, but its date and interpretation are not settled, and some scholars have proposed other readings.
Jesus died to bear human sin and to defeat the power of death. This is the New Testament’s interpretation of faith: history can confirm that He died, but cannot confirm for whom He died.
Where justice and love meet

Hundreds of years before the passion of Jesus, the book of Isaiah already described a suffering servant. Christians have used this passage to understand the cross from the very beginning; Jewish tradition mostly reads it differently.

But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
The order Paul describes is striking: it is not that we got better and then He came.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

Nor is this a helpless father and a helpless son. In Gethsemane He prayed, “let this cup pass away from me,” and His anguish was real; yet He also said with His own mouth that He laid His life down Himself.
No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”
The story did not stop on Friday. The resurrection turned the cross from an execution into a victory.
Put a nail in your pocket today, or hold one in your hand for a minute and feel how cold and hard it is. Slowly read Mark 15:29-32 and listen to what the people below were shouting.
Meditate: the people below shouted, “save yourself, and come down from the cross!” He could have come down, and He did not. What kept Him there?

Pray: Lord Jesus, You stayed there for me. I no longer have to buy Your love with my performance, and I no longer have to pretend I have no sin. I bring the thing I am most ashamed of to Your cross. Thank You for forgiving me, and from today make me die to myself and live to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: From self-centered to selfless: Paul says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” There is something today I must win at all costs, and I can set it down and make way.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: I can stand before God, and it is not by my merit. When others praise me, I remember who paid the price.

Carrying the cross does not mean putting up with violence: Jesus’ self-giving was a free act of love. It does not tell the abused to stay in danger. If you are suffering domestic violence or abuse, seeking safety and professional help is exactly what pleases God.

blocks.h: This week: write on a sheet of paper one piece of guilt you have carried for a long time, pray about it to God, read 1 John 1:9, and then tear the paper up. If it involves someone you owe an apology or restitution, talk with a spiritual companion about your next step.
Pass it on: “If there is a God, do you think He could wipe out all the evil in the world at no cost at all? Would that be fair to the victims?”
Quiz

quiz.q: Why is the discovery of Yehohanan’s remains important?
o: It proves every detail in the Gospels
It is rare physical evidence of first-century crucifixion
It proves where Jesus’ tomb was
quiz.e: It confirms that people were crucified at that time. It is not evidence about Jesus Himself, and its details are still being revised.

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of Roman crucifixion?
o: Public shaming and deterrence
Giving the condemned a chance to repent
Religious sacrifice
quiz.e: It was mostly inflicted on the lower classes and carried out in public places in order to deter.

quiz.q: In answering “cosmic child abuse,” what do evangelical scholars often stress?
o: Jesus did not really suffer
God the Father did not know about it
The Son was willing, and the Trinity worked together; He was not a helpless child
quiz.e: John 10:18 says, “I lay it down by myself.” At the same time, the cross must never be used to tell abuse victims to endure.

units.title: The Empty Tomb: A Question Mark That Frightened Everyone
units.sub: Paul left his own faith a way to be refuted. So this tomb is worth investigating.

share.v: But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruit of those who are asleep.

blocks.h: Paul left his own faith a way to be overturned. Writing to the believers in Corinth, he put it in the plainest terms:
If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith also is in vain.

So this tomb is worth investigating. And the first thing we run into is a surprise: Mary Magdalene, the first to discover the tomb empty, did not cheer, and it did not occur to her that Jesus had risen. She ran to report it.
“They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
A list sealed in amber

Paul wrote 1 Corinthians in about the 50s AD, yet in chapter 15 he says that what follows is something he “received”: that Christ died, was buried, and was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the twelve, more than five hundred brothers, and James. Paul is handing on a tradition older than the letter itself.

How much older? James Dunn holds that the tradition had already taken shape within months of Jesus’ death. Gerd Lüdemann, who does not believe in the resurrection, says within the first two years. Bart Ehrman cautions that working out such dates is not as precise as it looks: saying a passage is earlier than Paul’s letter does not mean it is earlier than his conversion. Most scholars still hold that its source lies only a few years from the event.

A tiny insect in amber is far older than the day the amber was picked up. This list is like that insect: the letter was written in the 50s, but the sentences sealed inside come from earlier years. The amber tells us that these people were preaching this very early, but it does not decide for us whether what they preached was true.
Three clues at the tomb

One: the tomb was recognizable. Mark says that Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, took the body and laid it in a tomb cut out of rock, and the women saw where it was placed. The archaeologist Jodi Magness considers the description consistent with burial practice in Jerusalem at the time, and also supports the detail that a rock tomb belonged to a family. Ancient sources do record cases of crucified people being taken down and buried. After reviewing the literature, John Granger Cook points out that the crucified were occasionally buried by family or by people concerned with the burial.

Two: the first witnesses were women. All four Gospels place women at the tomb. When Josephus restates the law in Antiquities 4.219, he says women are not to give testimony, on the ground that they are frivolous. The second-century critic Celsus also sneered at this: what was seen was only a half-hysterical woman. If someone were inventing a story to be believed, this would hardly be a clever casting choice. Richard Bauckham and Dale Allison both think real memory has been preserved here.

Three: the opponents’ reply. Matthew records a story that was going around: the disciples stole the body by night. Justin Martyr in the mid-second century mentions the same charge. This kind of rebuttal is an explanation of where the body went. This clue also has limits: it shows the direction of the dispute, but it does not prove that the opponents ever examined the tomb themselves.
This saying was spread abroad among the Jews, and continues until today.
The strongest case against
This section needs to be told in full, because these arguments really do have force.

items: The Romans aimed at humiliation. Ehrman holds that deterrence was one of the main points of crucifixion, and that rebels often did not receive an honorable burial; he suggests Jesus’ body was most likely handled hastily, perhaps thrown into a common grave, and says its actual fate cannot be known. John Dominic Crossan also argues that the disciples did not actually know what became of the body.

The layers of witness are thin. Matthew’s and Luke’s Joseph stories were most likely taken from Mark, so they do not count as independent multiple attestation; the creed Paul passed on says only “buried,” with no mention of Joseph; and Acts 13:29 can even be read as saying that the ones who condemned Him laid Him in the tomb.

The empty tomb appears late. Paul’s letters do not explicitly mention an empty tomb, and the earliest narrative is Mark, around AD 70, about forty years after the event. Richard Carrier argues that the earliest believers understood a “spiritual body,” and that the empty tomb was a later legend.
The details do not agree. The number of women at the tomb and whether there was one angel or two differ from Gospel to Gospel. Mark 16:8 even ends with the women saying nothing to anyone.

blocks.h: Others reply that the creed’s sequence is died, buried, raised, appeared, and that if the one who was buried was raised, it already implies the tomb no longer held a body. Allison also thinks concluding from Paul’s silence alone is not a strong enough argument. The women argument should not be stated too strongly either: a courtroom rule is not the same as everyday life in which women were never listened to.

items.n: The empty tomb is probably historical
