items.h: N. T. Wright holds that the empty tomb and the appearances must be taken together to explain why Jews began to proclaim “resurrection” at all. Without either one, neither can be explained.

items.n: The empty tomb is probably historical, but its meaning is another matter
items.h: Allison thinks Jesus was most likely laid in a tomb, that the women later found it empty, and that the story grew in the retelling; he also admits that these facts are not enough to compel anyone to a conclusion.

items.n: The empty tomb is probably legend
items.h: Ehrman holds that neither the burial nor the empty tomb can be known with certainty, and he also reminds us that an empty tomb does not by itself produce faith. Carrier and Crossan reach similar doubts by different routes.

blocks.h: The much-quoted 75%

You often hear that “about 75% of scholars accept the empty tomb.” The source is a 2005 article by the evangelical scholar Gary Habermas. He compiled more than 1,400 publications in German, French and English since 1975, and reported that among the works that address the question, about 75% favor at least one argument supporting the empty tomb, and about 25% hold arguments against.

Using this number requires four limits to be stated. First, he himself calls it a rough estimate, an informal barometer, and says plainly that the proportion cannot prove the resurrection. Second, this is one scholar counting publications, not a survey sample of scholars, and the denominator is not listed in the article. Third, the critic Taylor Carr pointed out in 2015 that the sample is selective and the raw data was not made public for checking. Fourth, authors who write on the resurrection are not a random sample of all scholars. From the pulpit, the most you can say is that one scholar’s compilation shows more works in favor than against, and that this still awaits independent verification.
Two archaeological stories not to misuse

One: the sealing stone. Amos Kloner argued that the stone at Jesus’ tomb was square and could only be pulled aside, not rolled. How this fits with the Gospels’ “rolled” is still under discussion. Two: the Nazareth Inscription. This stone tablet forbidding the disturbance of tombs was once used by some apologetics books as Rome’s reaction to an empty tomb. A 2020 isotope study indicated that the marble came from the Greek island of Kos, and the inscription itself never mentions Jesus, so the connection is very hard to sustain. Please stop citing it that way.
Take each of the following separately. The empty tomb cannot be called “established” by historical method, and we do not pretend it can.
1 Corinthians is a letter acknowledged as Paul’s own, and in 15:3-8 Paul himself says the tradition was something he “received.”

The source of this tradition is very early. Most scholars estimate it at only months to a few years from the event; the exact year cannot be worked out, and Ehrman also cautions against stating it too precisely.
Jesus was placed in a recognizable tomb. Allison, Magness and others support this; Ehrman and Crossan question it.

Women found the tomb empty on the first day of the week. Serious scholars can be found both among supporters and among skeptics; Habermas’s tally (about 75%) is an informal estimate that has not been independently verified, and cannot be treated as a vote count.

Whether the embarrassment of women as the first witnesses can serve as strong evidence is still disputed; the shape of the sealing stone is also unsettled; and a link between the Nazareth Inscription and Jesus most likely does not exist.

God raised Jesus from the dead. This is a confession of faith and also what we hold to be the best explanation; the historical method by itself cannot render this verdict. An empty tomb can have many explanations, and to reach this sentence we also need the witness of the appearances, our view of God, and personal trust.
The empty tomb, the Lord who calls by name
Mary stood before the empty tomb and found no comfort. She took the risen Lord for the gardener. What changed everything was a single call.
Jesus said to her, “Mary.”She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”

Here we see God’s faithfulness: He did not abandon the One who was crucified, and He did not abandon the one who wept. The apostles’ preaching puts the weight on what God did, and also sees God’s eternal power: not even death could hold Him.
whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it.

If the crucified Christ had stayed in the tomb, we would have only a remarkable martyr. Paul says His resurrection changed the end for everyone who has fallen asleep in Christ. This is hope prepared for those who have lost loved ones, and grace for those still in the dark today.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
Slowly read John 20:11-16. When you reach “Mary,” pause, put your own name in its place, and be quiet for a minute. Whatever you are weeping over, you can tell Him directly.
Meditate: is my faith more like standing at the tomb looking for a body, or have I already heard someone call my name? Am I willing to bring my lingering doubts before Him too?

Pray: Risen Lord, thank You for not staying in the tomb. My faith is often like Mary’s: I see, but I do not understand. Call my name, so that I turn around and recognize You. Comfort those who today are missing someone who has died. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: Paul dared to stake his faith on things that can be checked. I too can bring my questions before Scripture and the historical sources, and I do not need to inflate numbers for the sake of defending the faith.
God’s point of view: moving from “death has the last word” to “Christ is the first fruit.” The human, temporary view sees as far as the tomb door; God’s eternal view sees beyond it.
Let Jesus reign: if He really rose, He is more than a teacher I respect. There is something I am gripping today; I hand it over to this living Lord.

blocks.h: This week: read Mark 16:1-8 and John 20:1-18, and mark the similarities and differences in two colors. Take the one point that puzzles you most to a pastor or your small group.
Pass it on: “If you had to verify something that happened two thousand years ago, what kind of evidence would you most want to see? How do you think the empty tomb could be investigated?”
Quiz

quiz.q: When Mary Magdalene found the tomb empty, what was her first reaction according to John?
o: She thought someone had taken the Lord away, and ran to tell
She was immediately sure that Jesus had risen
She stayed where she was, waiting for angels
quiz.e: The empty tomb first brought confusion. She recognized the Lord when she heard Jesus call her name.

quiz.q: Regarding Habermas’s “about 75%” figure, which statement is the most honest?
o: It is a formal poll of New Testament scholars worldwide
It has proved the empty tomb to be a historical fact
It is his own rough estimate from compiling publications, and he himself says it cannot prove the resurrection
quiz.e: An informal barometer; critics also point to problems with the sample and with making the data public.

quiz.q: Which of the following should be marked as a philosophical and faith inference (c=4)?
o: 1 Corinthians is a letter of Paul
God raised Jesus from the dead
Matthew mentions a story of body-stealing
quiz.e: The first and last are facts about the documents. “God raised Him” goes beyond what the historical method can decide, and is a confession of faith.

units.title: The Disciples’ Transformation
units.sub: The same men who sat trembling behind a locked door stood in the open street about seven weeks later and spoke. What happened in between?

share.v: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.

blocks.h: On the evening of the third day after Jesus died, the door of that house was locked. The people inside had just lost their teacher, and they were afraid they would be next.

When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
About seven weeks later, in the same city, Peter, who only weeks before had sworn with curses that he did not know Jesus, stood up in public.
But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice and spoke out to them, “You men of Judea and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words.
Peter: from the charcoal fire to the council’s questioning

The Gospels do not cover for their leader. On the night Jesus was tried, Peter denied Him three times in the high priest’s courtyard, and in the end he wept. Later this same man was brought before the council, and said to the very people with the power to have him arrested, “we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” Those men saw that he was unlearned, and could not tell where his boldness came from.
James: the younger brother who once thought his older brother was mad

Jesus’ brother James is an even harder case to explain. John 7:5 says, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” Mark also remembers that when His friends heard about Him (the Chinese Union Version says “relatives”), they went out to seize Him, for they said, “He is insane.” Yet in Paul’s own letter to the Galatians he calls James “the Lord’s brother” and lists him among the “pillars” of the Jerusalem church. And what Paul passes on in 1 Corinthians 15:7 is only one short line: “Then he appeared to James.”

Historians outside the church mention him too. The Jewish historian Josephus records that around AD 62, after the Roman governor Festus had died and his successor Albinus was still on the road, the high priest Ananus took the opportunity to convene the council and hand over James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, together with others, to be stoned to death.

Imagine your older brother announcing one day that he is the Savior all humanity has been waiting for. Most likely you would first take him to see a doctor, and that was about the reaction of James’s family back then. A younger brother who grew up with him, who saw him lose baby teeth, get scolded and knock things over, is the hardest audience in the world to persuade.
Which martyrdom traditions hold up?

In sermons you often hear that “all twelve apostles except John were martyred,” but that goes too far. Sean McDowell’s The Fate of the Apostles examines the traditions one by one and finds a wide gap in the evidence: Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee and James the Lord’s brother have the strongest evidence; Thomas and Andrew come next; for several others the accounts are late and contradict one another, and his conclusion is that we do not know; as for John, he thinks a natural death is most likely.

Vivid details such as being crucified upside down or beheaded come mainly from apocryphal acts written from the second century onward, and they have a legendary flavor. The reliable early evidence is actually quite brief: 1 Clement, chapter 5, written around AD 95, mentions Peter and Paul suffering and bearing witness, but does not say how or where they died.

items.n: The evidence is enough to support the martyrdom of the central figures
items.h: McDowell holds that the martyrdoms of Peter, Paul and the two Jameses reach a high degree of historical probability, with early evidence from varied sources, but that nothing should be asserted about the others.

items.n: The evidence is thinner than the church imagines
items.h: Bart Ehrman holds that the sources are surprisingly few, and that all we can say is that Tacitus records Nero executing Christians, which makes the martyrdom of Peter and Paul a reasonable inference; the details are mostly later legend.

items.n: The martyrdom stories were shaped by later hands
items.h: Candida Moss argues that the early martyrdom accounts were all edited by later writers, and that systematic official Roman persecution lasted only a short time. Many Christian scholars criticize her method and conclusions, but she reminds us to be careful in citing such stories.

blocks.h: What can martyrdom prove?

Let us be honest: martyrdom cannot prove that a faith is true. People of every kind of faith in history have gone willingly to their deaths. McDowell himself says that these facts cannot prove the resurrection; they can only establish the sincerity of the apostles. The disciples could have been sincerely mistaken, and that is exactly the question the next unit takes up. What martyrdom can mainly rule out is one explanation: that the disciples knew it was false and made up the story. Also, the surviving sources rarely preserve the interrogations, so we mostly do not know whether they were offered a chance to “recant and live,” and that point should not be overstated either.

Paul also records that Peter later drew back out of fear of people at Antioch (Galatians 2). That is valuable: Peter’s transformation was real, yet it did not make him perfect. The legends that turn him into a saint came later, and in the earliest documents he still stumbles.
Separate what is certain from what is conjecture.
Galatians is among the letters scholars universally accept as Paul’s own, and in it he calls James “the Lord’s brother” and lists him with Cephas and John as the “pillars” of the church.
Tacitus records that Nero executed Christians after the fire of Rome. This is a record left by a non-Christian Roman historian.

Josephus, Antiquities 20.200, records that James was ordered stoned by Ananus around AD 62. Most scholars today regard this passage as authentic; the later version by Hegesippus (which has James thrown from the top of the temple) is more legendary and less credible.
1 Clement, written around AD 95, mentions the martyrdom of Peter and Paul and is the earliest testimony outside the Bible; details of place and manner come largely from later times.

The fates of the remaining apostles are mostly impossible to determine; McDowell judges Thomas more likely to have been martyred and John likely to have died naturally. Ehrman’s side and Moss are more skeptical of the whole tradition.

The most natural explanation for the disciples’ transformation is that they were convinced they had seen the risen Jesus and had received the Holy Spirit. This is an inference of faith: history can confirm only their conviction and their change, and cannot prove the God who gave the change.
He does not replace the weak; He moves in

After the resurrection, Jesus did not replace Peter, and did not settle accounts with him in public. For three denials there were three questions about his love, and each time He entrusted him with a work of shepherding.

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?”Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.”Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
Here we see God’s faithfulness: His promise does not depend on human performance. And the power that opened the door, the New Testament says, came from the Holy Spirit given by the risen Lord.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
The One who gave His life on the cross for Peter came back to find him after the resurrection. The Spirit who raised Jesus lives in those who believe in Him today.
But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
Recall the failure you would least like to have mentioned. Think of it as the pile of charcoal beside Peter, and then read John 21:17 once, putting your own name in place of “Simon.”
Meditate: how would Jesus ask me about the fall I most fear anyone finding out? Would He also put a task into my hands?

Pray: Risen Lord, like Peter I have made big promises, and I have also drawn back. Thank You for not replacing me. May Your Spirit live in me and open the door I have kept shut in my heart, so that I no longer depend on my own courage but on Your presence. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Holy Spirit is my guide: Peter’s boldness was not trained into him. Before deciding anything today, be still and ask: where does the Holy Spirit want me to go?

From self-centered to selfless: Peter once relied on his own resolve and said he would never fall; later he learned to say, “you know everything.” Set down the urge to prove myself and let Christ live in me.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry: Jesus first asked about Peter’s love before entrusting him with the flock. Before serving, return to my relationship with the Lord.

blocks.h: This week: find someone you have let down, or who has let you down, and write one sincere line of greeting or apology. If that relationship has brought harm or danger, do not force contact; bring it to God first and find a trusted person to walk with you.
Pass it on: “If the person closest to you suddenly said he had seen someone who had died and come back to life, what would have to happen for you to believe him?”
Quiz

quiz.q: Which statement about the “martyrdom of the twelve apostles” best matches McDowell’s research?
o: All twelve apostles have reliable martyrdom records
The evidence is strongest for Peter, Paul and the two Jameses, and uncertain for most of the others
There is no early evidence at all
quiz.e: The evidence varies widely. Only when we distinguish honestly is the testimony credible.

quiz.q: How does Josephus, Antiquities 20.200, introduce James?
o: As king of the Jews
It does not mention his older brother
As the brother of Jesus (called Christ)
quiz.e: This is a source from outside the Bible. Josephus was not a Christian, and he uses neutral wording.

quiz.q: What does martyrdom best show?
o: That the disciples sincerely believed what they preached
That Christianity has been proved true
That only Christians are willing to be martyred
quiz.e: Martyrdom establishes sincerity, which is not the same as proving truth. Whether they were mistaken must be examined separately.

units.title: Other Explanations for the Resurrection
units.sub: Stolen body, swoon, wrong tomb, grief visions, later legend. We try every key once, and see where our own key sticks.

share.v: When they saw him, they bowed down to him; but some doubted.

blocks.h: The first people to hear the news of the resurrection reacted much as most modern people do:
These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn’t believe them.

Even they did not believe it. So doubt is not a bad thing. The last unit left a question: even sincere disciples may have been sincerely mistaken. In this unit we invite the opposing side to lay out its best explanations, and we try the keys one by one.
Five keys

One: stolen or moved body. This is the oldest explanation. In the 18th century the German scholar Reimarus argued that the disciples stole the body and hid it in order to keep the resurrection claim alive. Today a weaker version that is harder to refute can be offered, and Richard Carrier discusses exactly the possibility that the body was moved by other people. Its difficulty is this: if the disciples knew it was fraud, it is hard to explain the price they later paid (see the last unit); and if unrelated persons moved the body, that explains the empty tomb but not the appearances.

Two: the swoon. Jesus did not really die, and revived in the cool of the tomb. In the early 19th century Paulus and Schleiermacher both supported similar views, and the Ahmadiyya tradition also holds this. What struck it down was David Strauss, who did not believe in the resurrection: a half-dead man needing bandages would at most make people think He had narrowly escaped, and would never make them believe He had conquered death. By the end of the 19th century few scholars accepted this view. A 1986 article in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) concluded that Jesus was already dead when taken down, but note that the article reasons from the Gospel descriptions and is not independent forensic evidence.

Three: the wrong tomb. Kirsopp Lake proposed in 1907 that, before dawn in an unfamiliar city, grieving women could have gone to the wrong place. This is not hard for anyone who sweeps graves today to imagine. The difficulty is that Mark says they had seen where He was laid, and that as soon as anyone went to the right tomb, the misunderstanding would be over. Like the stolen body, this key explains only the empty tomb.

Four: grief visions. This is the alternative explanation taken most seriously in scholarship today. Gerd Lüdemann and Ehrman both hold that Peter had a vision in his grief, and that others were then affected. The idea has real grounding: in 1971 W. Dewi Rees interviewed widows and widowers in mid-Wales, and about 14% said they had seen their deceased spouse, and nearly half had sensed the spouse’s presence. Experiences like this are common among the bereaved, and are not mental illness.

Five: later legend. The story grew with each telling, and the flesh-and-blood appearances were added later. Ehrman holds that at first there were only visions by a few people, who then persuaded the others. The difficulty is that the list in 1 Corinthians 15 is very early, and Paul himself says he saw Peter and James. Legend can explain the growth of details, but it is not easy for it to explain where the original conviction came from.

Imagine a door with four locks: the empty tomb, the appearances to Peter and others, the change in Paul, once an enemy, and the change in James, an unbelieving younger brother. Each explanation is a key. Some open the first lock easily, and then stick at the second. The other side will also remind us: why use only one key? A missing body plus grief visions might open two at once. That criticism is reasonable. What we must answer is whether two keys together are enough, and whether a key labeled “God” should also be laid on the table.
The strongest version of the vision theory and its difficulties

items.h: Dale Allison has collected a large number of accounts of the bereaved seeing the dead, and holds that the similarities are well worth studying, and there are even reports of several people seeing at once. He also cautions that saying “He appeared to the twelve” does not mean each one had the same experience, and that we know very little about the five hundred. Lüdemann even holds that Paul can be explained by inner conflict.

items.n: Visions are not enough to explain it
items.h: N. T. Wright points out that when Jews saw a vision of the dead, the usual conclusion was “his soul is still around,” never “he has been raised.” Paul was an enemy and James was at first an unbeliever, and neither was in the circle of grieving disciples. Bergeron and Habermas argued in 2015, from a clinical standpoint, that these psychological explanations do not fit present medical understanding. The reader should know that the latter is an apologist, and that the article is not the last word.

blocks.h: In fairness, Allison himself says that among the cases he knows, none is fully parallel to the whole resurrection event; he does not claim that visions explain everything, and he also says that apologists and skeptics both cannot do what they claim. This most widely read scholar leaves us with a humble pause.
What about cognitive dissonance?

Some also cite Leon Festinger’s 1956 When Prophecy Fails: when a prophecy fails, believers become even more zealous in spreading their message, and the disciples may have been the same. The classic study behind this explanation has itself come under question in recent years: Thomas Kelly, working from the archives, charges that the book’s central claim contains fabrication and exaggeration. This is a reminder for both sides: do not treat a popular analogy as settled.
The real watershed: prior probability

In the end the argument is often not about the sources but about prior assumptions. In 1748 David Hume argued that we should not accept a miracle unless the falseness of the testimony would be more incredible than the miracle itself. Later philosophers revised or criticized him with probability theory, for example John Earman; Timothy & Lydia McGrew argue that the evidence can greatly raise the probability of the resurrection. If one first decides that God does not exist or does not intervene, any natural explanation, however strained, beats the resurrection; if God exists, raising Jesus from the dead is no longer absurd. Michael Licona holds that historians may list the resurrection as the best explanation, while many historians think this goes beyond the tools of history.

Besides, accepting certain facts does not make one a Christian. The Jewish scholar Pinchas Lapide discussed the resurrection in a whole book, treating it as an experience of Jewish faith, yet he did not therefore acknowledge Jesus as Israel’s Messiah.
Every key has been taken up seriously by someone. We assess them separately, and admit that judgments come in degrees.

That the disciples deliberately stole the body and faked the resurrection is now accepted by very few scholars; however, the possibility that the body was moved by other people cannot be completely ruled out.

The swoon theory was abandoned by most scholars by the end of the 19th century. The main reason is the argument put forward by Strauss; the JAMA 1986 article is only a supplementary inference from the Gospels.
Sensing the presence of, or seeing, the dead after bereavement is a commonly documented experience, and is not the same as mental illness.

Whether grief visions can explain the experiences of Peter, the twelve, the five hundred, James and Paul is the heart of today’s debate, and there is no settled answer. The evidence for group visions is especially disputed.
Legend may indeed have played a role in the details of the story; whether it can account for how the earliest belief arose is judged differently by the two sides.

God raised Jesus from the dead: this is the answer we believe explains these clues most fully. This judgment depends on whether you allow that God exists and intervenes. Wise and honest atheists have looked at the same data and reached different conclusions; this should be admitted, and respected.
He goes toward the doubter

Matthew, at the climactic verse of the whole book, records that some still doubted. Scripture did not delete that line. John also preserves Thomas’s condition: he would not believe unless he touched the nail marks. When Jesus came back, He did not rebuke the condition; He met it.
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”

Here we see God’s faithfulness: He is not afraid of being examined, and He does not give up on the doubter. That the resurrected body still carries the nail marks, that the victorious Lord still bears the sign of the cross, is a wisdom we would never have imagined. What He stretched out to Thomas was the very hand that had been wounded for him.

When Paul spoke about the resurrection in Athens, he also met three reactions: some mocked, some said they would hear him again another time, and a few believed. He did not chase after the mockers to argue, and he did not inflate the numbers of those who believed.

Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.”Thus Paul went out from among them. But certain men joined with him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
Whichever of these three kinds of people you are today, you can listen once more.
Take a sheet of paper and write down your most honest doubt about the resurrection, without polishing it. Then, as Thomas did, bring that sheet to Jesus, and read John 20:24-29 once.
Meditate: is my doubt a real wish to know, or have I already decided not to know? And the other way around: is there somewhere my believing is afraid of being examined?

Pray: Lord Jesus, thank You for not leaving Thomas because of his doubt. I bring my questions to You. Show Yourself to me in Your own way, and give me a gentle and reverent heart toward friends who are still doubting. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: state the other side’s strongest argument better than they do, and only then give my own view. Honesty matters more than winning.
Jesus is my example: He stretched out His wounded hand to Thomas. With doubting friends, reach out the hand first, then speak.
People matter more than tasks: my goal is not to win a debate but to reach the person in front of me. A relationship outlasts an answer.

blocks.h: This week: find an article or video written by a skeptic, for example Ehrman on the resurrection, and watch or read it through carefully. Write down one point where you think he has a good case, and one question you want to look into further.
Pass it on: “About the resurrection of Jesus, what do you think is the most reasonable explanation? I would really like to hear your thinking.”
Quiz

quiz.q: Which alternative explanation is taken most seriously in scholarship today?
o: The swoon theory
Visions in grief
Jesus had a twin brother
quiz.e: Lüdemann, Ehrman and others argue in this direction, and visions among the bereaved are indeed common.

quiz.q: Who struck the hardest early blow against the swoon theory?
o: Christian apologists
The pope
Strauss, who himself did not believe in the resurrection
quiz.e: He pointed out that a half-dead man would not lead people to believe He had conquered death.

quiz.q: Why do wise people looking at the same sources reach different conclusions?
o: Because their prior assumptions differ, depending on whether they allow God to exist and intervene
Because the other side never read the sources
Because the sources have completely proved the resurrection
quiz.e: When historical reasoning reaches its end, it runs into questions of worldview. We should say this honestly.

units.title: Paul’s Conversion
units.sub: The man who threw members of the church into prison later became this faith’s most famous preacher. Thirteen of the New Testament’s twenty-seven books carry his name.

share.v: The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.

blocks.h: Imagine your church receives a notice: the man who has been throwing your brothers and sisters into prison is coming to preach next Sunday, and his topic is “Jesus is Lord.”
This really happened in the first century, and the man himself left a record in his own hand. Galatians records what the churches of Judea heard at the time.
but they only heard, “He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy.”So they glorified God in me.
We have his own handwriting

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry Paul’s name. Scholars almost unanimously accept seven of them as his own: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. The authorship of the others is still debated; many critical scholars think Ephesians and the Pastoral Letters come from later writers, and many evangelical scholars hold that they come from Paul.

This brings a rare advantage: his “conversion” does not rest only on what others reported. Galatians and Philippians are both among the undisputed seven, and in them are his own words: that “beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it,” that he was a Pharisee, and that “concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless.” E. P. Sanders, a scholar of Paul, estimates that the change took place around AD 33.
He turned the ledger over

An accountant moves the items in the asset column one by one into the loss column, and then says: the best closing of the books of my life. That is the picture Paul draws in Philippians. His bloodline, education and religious record are all still there; they have only changed columns.

The price he paid is listed in 2 Corinthians: five times whipped by the Jews, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked. There are no attractive benefits on this list. Tradition says he died in Rome; Sanders dates it to about AD 62 to 64.
What really happened on the road?

Paul says only that God was pleased “to reveal his Son in me,” and also, “Haven’t I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord?” Acts tells the story of the light and the voice three times. Both sides are sources, and they differ from each other: for example, Acts 9:7 says the men traveling with him heard the sound but saw no one, while Acts 22:9 says they saw the light but did not understand the voice. Scholars therefore treat the letters as primary and Acts as secondary; Sanders even says Acts sometimes conflicts directly with the letters.
How should we explain it? Several views are set side by side below.

items.h: The risen Jesus really appeared to him. Paul understood it that way himself, and he placed the event in the list of witnesses to the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:8).

Gerd Lüdemann and others hold that this was a real subjective experience, not an external event. Bart Ehrman puts the weight on the historical fact that the disciples had visions, and does not judge whether there was any reality behind them.

Some suppose that he was already shaken inside, or crushed by guilt. The difficulty is that what he describes about himself is “blameless,” and Krister Stendahl’s famous 1963 essay also points out that reading Paul as a man with a tormented conscience may be a later Western projection.

blocks.h: Was it a “conversion”?

Stendahl proposed that Paul did not change religion; he was called, like a prophet. Paula Fredriksen also avoids the word “conversion,” on the ground that he did not change gods and still considered himself a Jew; she points out that synagogue floggings were inflicted only on Jews, and that his five floggings show he stayed within that community. Alan Segal, from a sociological angle, keeps the label “convert.” N. T. Wright concludes that in one sense it was a calling, and in another sense it was also a conversion.

In 1977, Sanders’s Paul and Palestinian Judaism changed the discussion in this field, so that scholars no longer easily portray the Judaism of the time as a religion of earning salvation by works. So in telling Paul’s story we should not describe Judaism as a prison he escaped. This debate is still going on today, and evangelicals themselves do not evaluate it uniformly.
Paul’s story has his own handwriting, it has reports by others, and it has parts that still cannot be untangled.
In his early years Paul persecuted the followers of Jesus, and later became the preacher of this faith; this rests on his own account in his undisputed letters.
Scholars almost unanimously accept the authorship of seven Pauline letters.

The authorship of the Pastoral Letters (including 1 Timothy, shared in this unit) is disputed: many critical scholars think they are not in Paul’s own hand, and evangelical scholars mostly hold that they come from Paul. The self-description as “chief” of sinners fits the “least of the apostles” in his undisputed letters.
What exactly happened on the Damascus road cannot be fully determined by historical method; naturalists and theists interpret the same data differently.

His change was the personal intervention of the risen Christ, a sign of grace. This is an inference of faith; a person’s great transformation does not by itself prove that a faith is true, and other religions also have moving stories of transformation.
“Why do you persecute me?”
The words recorded in Acts deserve a longer pause. Saul was arresting disciples, yet the voice said: I am the Jesus you are persecuting. The wounds of the church, He counts as His own.
He said, “Who are you, Lord?”The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.”
Paul never forgot who he was all his life, and he was not crushed by that past.

For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
The source of this grace is the cross. He later wrote that he could live as he did because of a Lord who “loved me and gave himself up for me,” and who rose from the dead.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
On a sheet of paper write one name: the person you feel is the least likely in your whole life to believe in Jesus. It may be a relative, someone who hurt you, or yourself.
Meditate: do I have a list in my heart of people I have already given up on? What does God think of that list?

Pray: Lord Jesus, You appeared to a man who was persecuting You, and Your grace has no limit. You know all my past; free me from being bound by it, and from boasting in it. Remember the name I have written, and teach me, when You want to send me, to walk that road willingly as Ananias did. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: Paul threw his report card into the loss column. What is the column I most want to show to people?
From self-centered to selfless: “not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” Practice saying this when something gets done.
235 spiritual companions: without Barnabas to receive him, Saul might not have gotten through that door. Can I be a Barnabas to some newcomer?

blocks.h: This week: for seven days in a row, pray for the name you wrote down; and take the initiative to invite a newcomer, or someone who is often overlooked, for a cup of coffee. If the other person has hurt you, prayer is enough and you need not force contact; safety and boundaries are good things.
Pass it on: “Have you ever met someone whose change was so great you could hardly believe it? What do you think changed him?”
Quiz

quiz.q: How many letters do scholars almost unanimously accept as written by Paul himself?
o: Thirteen
Four
Seven
quiz.e: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon.

quiz.q: What does Stendahl remind us of?
o: Paul is more like a prophet who was called, and should not be read as a modern person with a tormented conscience
Paul did not exist
Acts has no value at all
quiz.e: His 1963 essay challenged the introspective Western reading of Paul.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe his righteousness under the law?
o: Always full of guilt
Blameless
He never studied the law
quiz.e: Philippians 3:6. This makes a simple guilt explanation difficult.

units.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
units.sub: After walking through all the evidence, He did not add another line. He asked only one question, and this question is in no hurry.

share.v: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”

blocks.h: Jesus took His disciples north to Caesarea Philippi, about 40 kilometers north of the Sea of Galilee. There is the cave of the god Pan there, and nearby a marble temple that Herod built for the Emperor Augustus; the city’s name pays tribute to Caesar.
Near this city full of the names of gods and emperors, He asked two questions. The first was easy. No one could dodge the second.

Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?”They told him, “John the Baptizer, and others say Elijah, but others, one of the prophets.”He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”
What “people say” today

The first question still has many answers today. According to a 2025 report by the Pew Research Center, in 2020 there were about 2.3 billion Christians worldwide (28.8%) and about 2 billion Muslims (25.6%), together more than half of the world’s population. The faith traditions of these people all speak seriously about Jesus. In other traditions too, there are people who hold Him in high regard.

Muslims honor Him as Isa, a prophet and messenger of God, born of the virgin Mary, who performed miracles, and the Qur’an also calls Him the Messiah. The same book says plainly that He was only a messenger, and also says that He was not killed and not crucified, but that God raised Him up to Himself.

The Jewish thinker Martin Buber said in Two Types of Faith (1951) that from his youth he had seen in Jesus his great brother, and that Jesus holds a lofty place in the history of Israel’s faith. But he acknowledged Him as a brother, not as the Messiah, and he held that the Jewish and Christian faiths are two different ways.

Among Buddhists, the Dalai Lama, in The Good Heart (1996), speaks of Jesus as a spiritually mature, good and warm person, and respects Christians’ understanding of Him; Thich Nhat Hanh also stresses His teaching and practice of nonviolence.
India’s Gandhi was deeply moved by the Sermon on the Mount (see Unit 5 of this hall), yet did not become a Christian.

A friend takes you to see a painting. One says it is a landscape, another says a portrait, and another says a forgery. You can respect every critic, and also admit that they cannot all be right. These tributes are sincere, but they do not describe the same Jesus: did He die on the cross? Was He a messenger, or the Lord? These answers cannot all be true at once. Real respect is not flattening someone else’s faith into your own shape.
The second question
He did not go on to ask, “And is your opinion the mainstream one?” What He asked was: “You.”

Peter answered correctly this time, but in the very next passage he took Jesus aside and urged Him not to suffer, and was sharply rebuked. So the first answer is often only a starting point: he had the title right, but did not yet understand its meaning.
Three paces in the Bible

items: Nicodemus: came by night with his questions (John 3:1-2), later spoke up for fairness toward Jesus (John 7:50-51), and finally brought spices to bury Him (John 19:39). He walked a long way.
The rich young man: after listening, he went away sorrowful. Mark writes first that “Jesus looking at him loved him,” and does not write that Jesus chased after him to pressure him (Mark 10:21-22).
The father who said “help my unbelief”: “I believe. Help my unbelief!” A half-and-half answer like this, Jesus did not turn away (Mark 9:24).

blocks.h: What is the response?

The response the New Testament speaks of can be put in three words: know who He is; repent, turning from a self-centered life back to God; and trust, entrusting your life to Him. This is less like passing an exam than like saying yes to a relationship. A next step is to look at “Life’s Questions Hall: How to Begin Walking with God.”

Historical verification can take you to the door; it cannot walk through for you. This is not an excuse that the evidence is insufficient, but because the question itself is more than a historical question. One who asks “Who do you say that I am?” wants an encounter.

People who have read the same evidence seriously have also given answers different from ours. When Paul spoke in Athens there were three reactions: mockery, “we’ll hear you another time,” and belief. All three kinds of people remain in Luke’s record.
In this last unit too, we must separate what is fact from what is faith.
The Pew Research Center estimates that in 2020 about 2.3 billion people worldwide were Christians, 28.8%, and 25.6% were Muslims.

The Qur’an calls Jesus the Messiah and a messenger, born of a virgin, and in 4:157-158 denies that He was killed or crucified; the Christian faith has the cross and the resurrection at its center. This is a real difference between the two traditions.
Caesarea Philippi lies at the foot of Mount Hermon and is known for its sanctuary of Pan; the tetrarch Philip made it his capital and named it in honor of Caesar.

Buber, the Dalai Lama, Thich Nhat Hanh and others express respect for Jesus, but none of that is the same as accepting the Christian confession; we cite them out of respect, and should not imply that they support the Christian faith.

Jesus is Lord; He died and rose, and this is God’s salvation. This is the Christian confession of faith. This hall offers reasons, not a formula. Each person must answer for himself, and has the right to disagree.
The One who asks has already come toward you
This question is not a cold exam. The One who asked it went on to tell His disciples that He was going to suffer, be killed and rise. What He was answering was in fact humanity’s greatest problem.

For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
His invitation is quiet, and very wide.
“Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
If you are willing to respond, the New Testament puts it very simply, so simply that you need not first have understood every question.
that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

If you want to pray, you can use your own words, or say this: “Lord Jesus, I believe You died for my sins and rose from the dead. I am willing to turn away from a self-centered life and give my life to You. Forgive me, and be my Lord. In Jesus’ name, amen.”
If you are not ready yet, this is also an honest prayer: “God, if You are really there, let me know.” Then keep investigating. There is no hurry, and no one is timing you.
Find a sheet of paper and write in the middle: “Jesus is ____.” You do not have to write the standard answer; write what you really believe today. You may write “I don’t know.”
Meditate: if He were sitting across from me now and asked, “Who do you say that I am?”, would the first thing that comes to mind be someone else’s answer, or my own?

Pray: Jesus, I no longer want to answer the question You asked with other people’s answers. You know my doubts, and You know my longing. Show Yourself to me, and lead me to the next step. I want to follow You and let You reign in my life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus reign: to confess Him as Lord is to let Him govern my money, my mouth, my schedule. Pick one thing to hand over to Him today.
The Holy Spirit is my guide: it is the Holy Spirit who lets people know Jesus, not my eloquence. In sharing the gospel I can set down the burden of “I must persuade him.”
People matter more than tasks: a friend is not a sales figure. Even if he says no for a lifetime, our friendship does not change because of it.

blocks.h: This week: If you have just made a decision: tell a Christian; start with the Gospel of John and read a passage each day; find a gathering, and look at “Life’s Questions Hall: How to Begin Walking with God.” If you are still thinking: finish reading the Gospel of John, write down your questions, and talk with a Christian you trust. If your family or place has pressure or danger around changing faith, proceed carefully and first talk with someone you trust; God watches over you.
Pass it on: “If Jesus were sitting across from you today and asked, ‘Who do you say that I am?’, how do you think you would answer? I’d like to hear what you really think.”
Quiz

quiz.q: What does Qur’an 4:157 say about the death of Jesus?
o: He was crucified and rose
He was not killed and not crucified
The text does not mention it at all
quiz.e: This is a real difference between Islam and the Christian faith, to be respected and not smoothed over.

quiz.q: When the rich young man walked away, how does Mark record that Jesus treated him?
o: He ran after him and scolded him
He told the disciples to stop him
He looked at him and loved him, and let him go
quiz.e: Mark 10:21-22. Jesus’ invitation was sincere, not pressure.

quiz.q: What happened after Peter correctly answered “You are the Christ”?
o: He immediately took Jesus aside and urged Him not to suffer, showing he did not fully understand yet
He instantly became a perfect man
Jesus never spoke to him again
quiz.e: The first answer is often only a starting point.

Did Jesus really exist in history?

sub: From the Jesus of history to the empty tomb: twelve units weighing the evidence and arriving at the question: Who do you say I am?
